Memorandum of Conversation, by the Director of the Office of Near Eastern Affairs (Hart)

div.head:
No. 907
Memorandum of Conversation, by the Director of the Office of Near Eastern Affairs (Hart)

list.item: General Mahmoud Riad, Head of the Arab Section, Egyptian Foreign Ministry and member of Egyptian Delegation to the General Assembly
Mr. Parker T. Hart, Director, NE

div.p: General Riad raised the question of the Bat Galim and asked what I thought of Israel’s action in attempting for the first time to send a vessel flying the Israeli flag through the Suez Canal. I replied that Israel had openly stated that this was a test case. “But testing for what?” asked Riad, “Could they possibly imagine that we would permit a vessel flying this flag to transit the canal?” General Riad expressed his view that the Israel Government was attempting to throw a monkey wrench into the final stages of the British-Egyptian negotiations.

While agreeing that this might be one motive for Israel’s reaction, I felt more inclined to believe that the Israel Government had sent the Bat Galim in the belief that she would be seized and with the intention of forcing the hand of the United States on a matter of principle involving Suez Canal traffic. I said that Israel had for some time been pushing the U.S. Government to intervene in the Anglo-Egyptian negotiations of the matter of Suez Canal traffic. The U.S. Government had felt, however, that the Egyptian Government was actually dropping restrictions on traffic. I understood that a lot of cargo was being allowed to pass through the Canal to Israel. General Riad replied: “Not a lot, all cargo.” He personally had kept an accurate record made of cargo shipment to or from Israel which had transited the Canal during several months. The Egyptian Government had not interfered since all traffic was under non-Israel flag. Egypt, however, could not permit a vessel flying the Israeli flag to enter her territorial waters and would insist on her rights in this respect under Article 10, in view of Arab opinion.

I indicated that the United States was not anxious for the principle of freedom of transit to once again come before the Security Council. However, should the principle again be an issue for Council vote, I could not see how the United States could do otherwise than go right down the line supporting the Convention of 1888 and the Security Council Resolution of 1951. I remarked that this had nothing to do with Zionist pressures in this country but was a position which we and most maritime nations of the world had taken long ago on the meaning of the Convention of 1888. Egypt was therefore likely in such a case to find most of the Western world voting against her.

Riad replied that he understood our position. If Egypt were forced to choose between the approval of the West and the approval
of the Arab nations, she would unquestionably choose the latter. However, he felt that there was room for further discusion on an interpretation of the Convention of 1888 and of the Egyptian Armistice Agreement with Israel. He believed that Egypt had good grounds for asserting that Israel flag vessels could not enter her territorial waters. They might carry cargoes of explosives or otherwise endanger Egypt’s security. If Egypt were to search such vessels, this would also be protested as interference. How, therefore, was Egypt to protect herself except by exclusion? He wanted my views regarding cargoes of weapons and munitions.

I replied that we were now getting into technicalities which I would have to investigate further before I could reply. However, I wished to reassert my belief that the United States would have to continue its strong stand for freedom of transit if the Bat Galim case became an issue of principle in the Security Council. We would not feel that because Egypt disliked the flag a vessel was flying, she was entitled to forbid her to transit.
